outcome: Chess is still unsolved: no one has established the perfect-play value of the standard starting position, and the English Wikipedia 'Solving chess' article (revision footer 9 September 2026) still says no complete solution is known in either the ultraweak or the weak sense. Since 26 January 2024 the events are endgame tablebase progress (a partial 8-piece release on Lichess, dated 7 February 2026, and two finished 8-piece tables reported on TalkChess in May 2026), an informal individual claim that chess is a draw under perfect play (TalkChess, 12-15 August 2024) whose author conceded it is not a rigorous proof, and a theoretical arXiv preprint (arXiv:2607.09715, June 2026) on a never-losing search that does not state chess's value. No AI system is credited with any result on this problem.
problem_asks: The statement asks one thing: the outcome of a perfectly played game of chess, from the standard initial position. That outcome is one of three values: a win for White, a win for Black, or a draw. Read strictly, this is an ultraweak question (the value only, with no strategy). Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' article treats 'solved' more broadly, so two further parts are named here for the judging pass to weigh, though the statement does not ask for them explicitly: (a) a weak solution, meaning a strategy from the initial position that achieves the value against any opponent; (b) a strong solution, meaning an optimal move in every reachable position. The parenthetical 'See also first-move advantage in chess' points at whether the first move wins by force, which is one reading of part (a) of the outcome question, not a separate question. Nested-bullet note: the parent bullet is 'Chess:' with no statement content, so nothing is inherited from it.

events.what_happened: On TalkChess, forum user jefk (named Jef Kaan in a search summary; not confirmed on the forum) posted a 'very rough and preliminary' draft for arXiv titled 'Chess is solved'. The first post, 12 August 2024 at 9:38 pm, says 'I present an ultraweak solution for the game of chess, indicating that it is a draw', ending 'QED, chess is a draw (with perfect or at least adequate play). Thus, it is ultraweakly solved.' It adds a 'tentative' weak solution resting on engine and correspondence-chess results, and calls the strong solution 'an open challenge'. The argument is posted in a thread titled 'proof' (locked). The forum-search title of the same thread is 'so below there's a (very rough and preliminary) a draft preprint for arxiv or so proving chess is solved'. I found no arXiv posting of this draft.
events.delivers: Claims, informally, that from the initial position the perfect-play value is a draw (neither side can force a win), so an ultraweak solution in the sense of value only. The argument as posted uses backward induction and abductive reasoning from the structure of the game tree, supported by empirical evidence (engine and correspondence results, a Chinese database, and TCEC-style draws). The weak solution is explicitly tentative. Restriction: the author himself says the reasoning is not a rigorous proof.
events.remains: Everything it does not rigorously establish: a proof of the draw value (the author conceded on 13 August 2024 that it is 'not a rigorous math proof (yet)'); any strategy from the start (the weak solution, which the author calls tentative); and the strong solution, which the author calls 'an open challenge'. It does not address the win-for-White or win-for-Black possibilities beyond the informal argument.

checked_by.what_they_did: Agreed chess is drawn but said the argument is inductive reasoning, not proof by induction, and 'falls below the exalted level of a proof'. A critique, not a verification.
Said 'By definition, you have not ultraweakly solved anything, as you haven't provided a rigorous proof.' A critique, not a verification.
Used an elephant analogy ('So now we have 100 grey elephants') and said it is 'Still not a proof, if there is a single pink one somewhere else.' A critique, not a verification.

Called the claim 'worthless', challenged the definition of 'ultra-weak solution', and asked how the databases and engines could be sure they had missed nothing. A critique, not a verification. Posts of 14-15 August 2024 in the thread 'proof'.

events.time_since_posted: About 26 months (August 2024 to October 2026). The last post in the thread I read is 15 August 2024 and the thread is locked. I found no later post or paper by the author on this claim.
events.doubts: (1) The author's own concessions. On 13 August 2024: 'For the skeptics ok it's not a rigorous math proof (yet), I now agree', and the reasoning 'still contains a -minor- logical hole', with a hypothetical White win after about 200 moves that his mate-avoidance argument might miss. He called the reasoning abductive, saying it 'does not definitively verify' the conclusion. (2) On 15 August 2024 he wrote 'i don't think i'm going to present such reasoning and/or results. At least not here.' and 'Ergo end of discussion.' (3) Every critic in the thread says the argument is not a proof. (4) The evidence cited is empirical (engine and database results, draws in engine matches) and does not exclude a deep forced win for either side, which is the central gap. (5) The author disputes the definition of 'ultraweak', while critics cite the standard definition. The author's own clarification was that the title 'could better have been a tentative proof'.
events.direction: Says the start is a draw under perfect play, so neither side can force a win. If correct, this would answer the outcome question as a draw. It is an informal argument, not a proof.
people: jefk (forum handle; Jef Kaan per a search summary)

events.what_happened: A TalkChess thread titled 'Chess is a Draw' (101 posts; I read page 8, which does not include the opening post) carries informal arguments in May 2024. The earliest post I saw is 5 May 2024. Uri Blass wrote: 'I believe nobody is going to prove in the next 10 years even that chess is at least a draw for white.' jefk argued from a claimed weakly dominant strategy for White and from 'balanced game' intuition, and suggested 'AlphaZero-derived knowledge' could show White cannot force a win. Jouni reported 100 draws in 100 engine games (Stockfish and Lc0, with no book) as 'SF and Lc0 plays perfect chess from opening position'. No proof is offered.
events.delivers: No result. Intuition, empirical engine draws, and an argument from a claimed weakly dominant strategy for White. Uri Blass says that argument is not a proof because zugzwang can defeat it in some symmetric positions.

checked_by.what_they_did: Argued the weakly-dominant-strategy argument is not a proof, because zugzwang can make the side to move lose in some symmetric positions. A critique, not a verification.

events.direction: Informal support for a draw under perfect play. The thread makes no claim that counts as a result.

events.what_happened: Lichess (the site's official account, built with Marc Bourzutschky and Niklas Fiekas) released 'op1', a partial 8-piece endgame tablebase covering 8-piece positions with at least one white pawn and one black pawn that oppose one another. It is downloadable (63 TiB), queryable through an API, and available on the analysis board and mobile app. The Lichess blog post is dated 7 February 2026. Wikipedia's 'Endgame tablebase' article dates the creation of op1 to 2025.
events.delivers: Exact tablebase values (win, draw and loss, with distance) for the op1 subset of 8-piece endgames, about 5.0 x 10^14 legal positions. Wikipedia's 'Endgame tablebase' article says this is about 1.3% of all 8-piece positions. The Lichess post says about half of 8-piece endings reached in practical games fall in op1, checked against game databases. Restrictions: endgame positions only, defined by the opposing-pawn-pair condition; no statement about the starting position.
events.remains: The outcome of the full game from the standard start; the rest of the 8-piece positions (outside op1, about 98.7% by Wikipedia's count); all positions with 9 or more pieces; any weak or strong solution.
events.time_since_posted: About 8 months. The release has been discussed on TalkChess and in Lichess comments, and IRL Chess ran a column on it (16 February 2026, seen only as a search summary), but I found no independent check of the table values.
events.direction: A partial solution of a class of 8-piece endgames. It does not bear on the outcome from the start.

events.what_happened: On 18 May 2026 a TalkChess user 'syzygy' posted a Linux-only tool to generate and compress 8-piece endgame tables on ordinary hardware. The 7- and 8-piece files use a new layout that existing Syzygy probing code cannot read. On 21 May 2026 the same user reported two finished 8-piece tables, KNNNNNNvK and KNNNNvKRR (the latter took about 5 hours 40 minutes with a RAM disk), projected about 12.5 days per largest pawnless table, and estimated the complete WDL+DTZ 8-piece set at 1.5 to 2 PB. The author wrote that completion is 'not going to happen anytime soon, if ever'. A reply on 29 May 2026 (Koistinen) estimated about 5 hours per table, which the author called 'definitely way too optimistic'.
events.delivers: Two more 8-piece endgame tables (KNNNNNNvK and KNNNNvKRR) are generated, and a generator is released. The claims are about endgame tables, not the starting position.
events.remains: The rest of the 8-piece set, all positions with 9 or more pieces, and the outcome from the start.
events.time_since_posted: About 5 months. Forum replies on feasibility (29 May 2026) exist, but I found no independent verification of the two tables.
events.doubts: Self-reported progress from the generator's author on a forum. The author's own timing figures were disputed in the thread, and the 8-piece count and table sizes are rough estimates.
events.direction: Advances the 8-piece endgame frontier. Does not bear on the start.
people: syzygy (TalkChess user; identity not stated in the thread)

events.what_happened: Fabio Romano, 'How to program a never-losing chess engine', arXiv:2607.09715 (cs.GT). v1 submitted 24 June 2026; v2 submitted 3 August 2026 (the current version). It proposes a graph-theoretic model of finite two-player perfect-information games, a backtracking minimax search that marks vertices as wins (a game-resolution search), and a variant that tests whether a named player can always avoid losing (reach at least a draw) from the initial position. The abstract disclaims practical speed: the aim is to prove formally, at least in theory, that such a strategy is possible. It does not state chess's value.
events.delivers: Per the arXiv HTML version, read through a summarising fetch and not by me reading the theorems directly: Theorem 3.4 says that if the search is run and eval(start)=g, the search marks the start as a win for g. Theorem 4.8 says that if a path from the start ends at a vertex v and every vertex on it is marked NIL after the search, then eval(v) is not g, which gives moves that secure at least a draw 'provided that the strategy is adopted starting from the initial position'. These statements are conditional on running the search, which the paper says is not practically feasible. They do not establish chess's value.
events.remains: The value of the standard start (win for White, win for Black, or draw). Which player g is, is not identified in the statements I read. Whether the search can be executed on chess is not addressed. The weak and strong solutions are untouched.
events.time_since_posted: About 3.5 months. I found no commentary on it in my searches.
events.doubts: (1) Single-author arXiv preprint; I found no peer review or expert comment. (2) The author's own abstract says the algorithm is not expected to find the strategy in practice, so the existence result is theoretical. (3) My reading of the theorems is second-hand: the PDF fetch returned binary content I could not read, and the HTML was summarised by a fetch tool. (4) A third-party copy I saw carries a 14 July 2026 header, while arXiv lists 24 June 2026 for v1; this is unexplained. (5) By Zermelo's theorem, at least one side always has a strategy that avoids losing in a finite game like chess, so a never-losing result only adds information when it is tied to a specific player and to the starting position. The HTML summary says it is, but I could not confirm which player.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on the value. If the draw-strategy statement applies to the start for a named side g, it establishes a restricted piece of the outcome: that g can avoid losing from the start. It does not say whether g wins or only draws.

events.what_happened: Mehmet Mars Seven, 'New Approaches to Strategic Thinking in Dynamic Games', arXiv:2609.21163 (econ.TH), submitted 18 September 2026, one version, 34 pages. The abstract mentions chess once: one proposed approach is 'inspired by how chess players reason in sequential games'. A search snippet described this paper as showing that the threefold-repetition and fifty-move rules do not change chess's game-theoretic value. The abstract I opened says nothing of the kind, so either the snippet describes different text or the full paper makes that claim. I did not read the full text.
events.delivers: Per the abstract: models of strategic choice in dynamic games (historical equilibrium, simple Nash equilibrium, cautious backward induction), with no claim about chess's value. The snippet's claim that repetition rules leave the value of chess unchanged is unverified.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, on the abstract. If the snippet's claim is in the full text, it concerns the rules variant rather than the outcome of the standard game.
events.direction: Not about chess's value, per the abstract. The discrepancy with the snippet is unresolved.

events.what_happened: Matthew Bolan and Andreas Tsevas, 'Universality of Infinite Chess', arXiv:2602.14277, submitted 15 February 2026 (math.LO, cross-listed to math.CO). It shows that infinite chess on an infinite board is as expressive as possible: every open Gale-Stewart game with draws is strategically equivalent to some infinite-chess position, and every countable ordinal arises as a game value. A third-party AI-generated review (The Moonlight, seen only as a search snippet) reads the paper as settling the supremum of game values as omega-1; that is the reviewer's reading, not the authors'.
events.delivers: Game values of infinite-board chess on Z^2: all countable ordinals are realised. Restriction: the infinite board, not the standard 8x8 game.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The paper says only that 'all game values of chess are countable' as a general statement and does not analyse the standard starting position.
events.time_since_posted: About 8 months. The only engagement I found is the AI-generated third-party review, which I did not open.
events.direction: Different problem: infinite-board chess. It does not bear on the outcome of standard chess. Discounted.

events.what_happened: Gardner's 5x5 minichess was weakly solved as a draw (arXiv:1307.7118). Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' article (opened) states this. The arXiv page itself was not opened; the date comes from the arXiv identifier (July 2013) and a search snippet.
events.delivers: The game-theoretic value of the 5x5 Gardner minichess variant (a draw), as a weak solution. Restriction: a 5x5 variant, not standard chess.
events.time_since_posted: About 13 years. I did not check reviews or citations for it.
events.direction: Analogue (a smaller variant). It settles nothing about standard chess. Discounted.

events.what_happened: Losing chess (antichess) was weakly solved as a win for White from 1.e3 by Mark Watkins. Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' article (opened) says the variant was weakly solved as a win for White. A search summary of Watkins's own page gives the completion as 1.e3 b6 announced in October 2016, after 1.e3 c5 in February 2015. I did not open Watkins's page, so the exact day is not used here.
events.delivers: A weak solution of the Losing Chess variant (a win for White from 1.e3), dependent on the stalemate rule set used. Restriction: a variant, not standard chess.
events.time_since_posted: About 10 years. I did not check reviews.
events.direction: Analogue (a variant). It settles nothing about standard chess. Discounted.

events.what_happened: The Lomonosov DTM endgame tablebases for 4+3 and 5+2 material were generated on the Lomonosov supercomputer at Moscow State University and completed in 2012, at about 140 TB. Wikipedia's 'Endgame tablebase' article (opened) lists them as completed in 2012, and says they were attacked by ransomware in 2021 and have been offline since. A search summary credits Makhnychev and Zakharov and gives July and August 2012 for the two sets; I did not verify these.
events.delivers: Exact distance-to-mate values for the 4+3 and 5+2 material types. Together with other sets (Syzygy), Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' lead says all non-trivial endgames with at most seven pieces or pawns are covered. Restriction: endgames only.
events.remains: The outcome from the start, and every position with 8 or more pieces.
events.time_since_posted: About 14 years. The set has been offline since 2021, per Wikipedia.
events.direction: Endgame coverage, not the start. It is baseline context, not a result on the problem.

events.what_happened: The Syzygy tablebases, generated by Ronald de Man and Bojun Guo, cover all seven-piece positions in compressed form. Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' article (opened) says the Lomonosov set's 140 TB was later reduced to 18.4 TB through Syzygy. The 2018 date comes from a search summary of python-chess documentation and the EPFL concept page, which I did not open.
events.delivers: Compressed WDL and DTZ values for all positions with up to seven pieces. Same coverage as Lomonosov, no new result about the start.
events.remains: The outcome from the start, and every position with 8 or more pieces.
events.direction: Endgame coverage, not the start. Context only.

events.what_happened: Marc Bourzutschky announced results from first explorations into 8-piece territory in 2021, per the Lichess op1 post (opened). A May 2021 chess.com blog summary by Rocky64 (a mirror on ozproblems.com is dated 28 May 2021; not opened) reports a longest pawnless 8-piece forced win of about 400 moves, and that Haworth's Law may not hold at this stage.
events.delivers: Partial 8-piece coverage, with an initial longest-pawnless-win figure of about 400 moves (later superseded). No completed 8-piece table set.
events.remains: The outcome from the start; the full 8-piece set.
events.direction: Endgame progress, not the start. Context only.

events.what_happened: Marc Bourzutschky found an 8-piece forced win of 584 moves, ignoring the 50-move rule, in mid-2022. Wikipedia's 'Solving chess' article (opened) lists it as the longest known as of January 2023 and says the 8-piece tablebase is incomplete, so 584 may not be the maximum.
events.delivers: One record length of a forced win in one 8-piece endgame, ignoring the 50-move rule. Restriction: endgame only.
events.remains: The outcome from the start; the full 8-piece set.
events.direction: Endgame record, not the start. Context only.

disputes.summary: Whether the August 2024 TalkChess draft counts as a solution. Its author calls it an ultraweak solution, the value being a draw, based on informal reasoning and empirical evidence. Every critic in the thread, and the author's own later concessions, say it is not a proof. No credit or priority dispute was found.

summary: Chess is unsolved as of the latest source I opened: the English Wikipedia 'Solving chess' article (revision footer 9 September 2026), which says no complete solution is known in either the ultraweak or weak sense and that progress 'is extremely limited'. Nothing I found since 26 January 2024 settles the outcome from the standard start. The in-window events fall in three groups. (1) Endgame tablebases: Lichess's partial 8-piece release 'op1' (blog dated 7 February 2026; about 5.0x10^14 positions, which Wikipedia's endgame page puts at about 1.3% of 8-piece positions) and a TalkChess report from May 2026 that a new generator had finished two 8-piece tables. Its author says the full set is 'not going to happen anytime soon, if ever'. These are endgame results and do not move the start. (2) An individual's informal claim: on TalkChess (12-15 August 2024) jefk argued that chess is a draw under perfect play, calling it an ultraweak solution and a tentative weak one. The argument rests on backward induction and empirical engine and database evidence. He conceded in the thread that it is 'not a rigorous math proof (yet)' and that the reasoning 'still contains a -minor- logical hole'. Critics said it is not a proof, and he closed the discussion saying he would not present it 'at least not here'. I found no paper, peer review, or later citation. This is the event closest to the question, and it is informal. (3) A theoretical preprint: Fabio Romano, arXiv:2607.09715, 'How to program a never-losing chess engine' (24 June 2026; v2 3 August 2026). It gives a backtracking minimax search, correctness and completeness statements, and a draw-strategy statement for a named player from the initial position. Its own abstract says the algorithm is not expected to run in practice, and it does not state chess's value. I read the theorems only through a summarising fetch of the HTML version, because the PDF returned binary content, so the statements and the identity of the player are unverified by me. Close call: if the draw-strategy statement really applies to the start for a named side, it is a partial piece of the outcome (that side cannot lose), not the value. The 2024 draft is informal, and the 2026 preprint is conditional on an infeasible search, so I did not treat either as a settlement. Pre-window events give context: Lomonosov DTM 4+3 and 5+2 (2012), Syzygy seven-piece coverage (2018), 8-piece explorations (2021), and a 584-move 8-piece forced win (2022). The variants Gardner 5x5 minichess (weakly solved as a draw, 2013) and Losing Chess (weakly solved as a win for White, 2016) are analogues and say nothing about standard chess. Infinite-board chess (arXiv:2602.14277, February 2026) is a different problem. arXiv:2609.21163 (September 2026) mentions chess only as an inspiration in its abstract, although a search snippet described it as settling the repetition-rule question. I could not confirm that from the abstract. Dates: Wikipedia's endgame page dates op1 to 2025 (the creation collaboration), while the Lichess post is dated 7 February 2026. I used the post date as the first public date. AI: no AI system is credited with a result on this problem. I searched for it directly. LLM chess-solving claims turned up only benchmarks and playing-strength results. 'AI proves chess draw' found only the 2007 checkers result. The 2026 lab announcements I found (OpenAI's 1 August 2026 'Astra' list of ten results, per a GIGAZINE report, since OpenAI's page returned 403) contain no chess problem. A Bloomberg feature of 27 March 2026 argues that AI-driven engine play has made top-level chess drawish. It is a practice observation, not a result, and I read only excerpts because the page returned 403. Elon Musk's 3 September 2026 post that chess 'will be fully solved one day' is a prediction, not an event. The May 2024 TalkChess thread quotes ChatGPT-4 discussions (in a post summarised by my fetch tool; I did not read the quoted exchange) and jefk floats 'AlphaZero-derived knowledge' as intuition. Neither produces a result, so I recorded that thread with none_found false and no systems. Parent bullet 'Chess:' has no statement content, so nothing is inherited.
competing_reading: Read the August 2024 TalkChess argument, with its empirical support, as an informal ultraweak solution (the value is a draw), and read Romano's June 2026 preprint as a genuine, if partial, outcome result: a named side can avoid losing from the start. On that reading the problem has moved since 2024, in a restricted way. Against it: the 2024 author conceded the argument is not rigorous and stopped; the 2026 paper does not claim a value and its theorems are conditional on a search it says is not feasible; and the endgame events do not reach the start. A further reading treats the Romano statement as a trivial consequence of Zermelo's theorem, which would make it uninformative about the value.
what_would_settle_it: For the 2024 claim: a rigorous, checkable proof of the draw value (a certificate or an expert verification of the argument), or a published critique that settles the 'logical hole'. For the Romano preprint: a direct reading of the theorem statements, the identity of the named player g, whether the draw-strategy statement covers the initial position, and any expert review. For endgames: nothing bears on the start unless the full 8-piece set or a proof from the start appears. For AI: an authors' statement crediting an AI system with any part of an argument on the start's value; none exists in what I found.
